36th Annual Graham & Dodd Luncheon Transcript 
 
Date: October 5th, 2026 
Location: Metropolitan Club, New York City 
 
Moderator: Prof. Tano Santos, the Robert Heilbrunn Professor of Asset Management and 
Finance and the Academic Director of the Heilbrunn Center for Graham & Dodd Investing at 
Columbia Business School 
Speaker: Li Lu '96 (’96 CC,’96 LAW), Founder and Chairman of Himalaya Capital 
 
Fireside Chat 
Tano: Thank you so much. I know you guys are incredibly excited to be here, and I know it’s not 
because of me, but rather because of our guest today, who I will introduce shortly. 
Before we start with the interview, let me take a couple of minutes to tell you that, as always at 
this time of year, the Heilbrunn year is up and running in full swing. The students, some of 
whom are here, have already taken my Modern Value class. They’re taking the Applied Value 
Investing class, their Credit Superhighway, all the electives. We’re having a blast. They’re all 
absolutely wonderful. 
In addition, we have a new initiative this year in the Heilbrunn Center. We launched our first 
Global Value Investor program, and the first cohort of that program, a joint effort with Columbia 
Business School Executive Education, is here. These are all the wonderful friends from China 
who are visiting us this year. Thank you so much for being here. 
Michael [Mauboussin] and I — I get asked this question a little too often — are already working 
on a new season of the Value Investing with Legends podcast. Episodes will be coming soon, so 
that is something to look forward to. 
 
Page 2 
We made our new stock selections for the student portfolio, the Tom Russo student portfolio. 
What did we buy this year? Equifax, Humana. What else? We bought the great Japanese bicycle 
company, Shimano, a classic value play if there was one; Copart, an online auction company; 
Perimeter Solutions, fire solutions [company]. A lot of fun things. As always, you can download 
all the reports the students have done over the years on the different companies. It’s a 
wonderful resource, and I very much encourage you to look at that. 
I want to single out a wonderful member of our community. I’m always amazed by Tom Russo’s 
generosity with the Heilbrunn Center, not only because of the student portfolio, but because of 
everything he does for the program, and in particular this year, making sure that our friend Li Lu 
could be here, for which we’re always thankful. 
We just had a wonderful week, as I told you a moment ago. With this new program, the Global 
Value Investor program, Andrew Gundlach and Kristin Gilbertson put on a show for them, which 
I also want to acknowledge publicly. 
Finally, we’re getting ready for a terrific CIMA conference. It’s amazing, the names that are 
coming this year. We’re going to have Howard Marks, Bill Ackman will be there, Josh Wolfe of 
Lux Capital will be there, Samantha McLemore from Patient Capital. I very much hope to see 
many of you there. 
Now, to the main event. Li Lu, of course, needs no introduction, as he’s truly one of the great 
modern value investing legends. He’s the founder and chairman of Himalaya Capital, which he 
founded in 1997. He has built an enormous record of performance in the last 30 years. 
Li Lu, as many of you know, is one of our most distinguished alums. He graduated with a law 
degree, an MBA degree, and a BA from Columbia College, because why get just one degree 
when you can get three? Apparently, this was how he thought about it. His personal story is well 
known. I won’t repeat it here. Li Lu is famous as an early investor in BYD and many of the great 
Chinese names, and we’ll have the opportunity to discuss issues related to the Chinese stock 
market today. 
First of all, Li Lu, welcome, and thank you so much for being here. 
Li Lu: Thank you, Tano. 
Tano: I’m going to talk for about 15 minutes, and then I’ll open it up for questions. I’m going to 
ask you to keep them short and to the point, and I will be ruthless. If you take more time than I 
consider necessary to get your point across, I’ll cut you off and give you a nasty look. Keep them 
short, because I’m sure there will be many questions. 
Li Lu, I want to start here. As I said, you are one of the great names in modern value investing. 
You’re deeply intertwined with the story of value investing at Columbia Business School. We 
were talking about that over lunch. You were there at the very beginning when Bruce was 
 
Page 3 
launching this program. We know of your friendship and partnership with Charlie and Warren, 
and how many things you guys did together. 
We will be celebrating 30 years of the founding of Himalaya Capital next year, which is a 
remarkable achievement. I want to start here. I want you to tell us a little bit: What have you 
learned about value investing, and where do you think we are today? What is the thing you wish 
you had known at the beginning? What is the lesson we have now that we didn’t have when you 
were studying these ideas at Columbia Business School? 
Li Lu: Thank you, Tano. First of all, thank you all for being here. It is such a wonderful occasion. 
Back when I was a student, as well as a young professional, I also attended a few of those 
luncheons. It was the highlight. I hope I do some justice now, 30 years later. 
The discipline of value investing started with Columbia. When Ben Graham first started his 
classes, it was almost 90 years ago. Of course, he practiced 10 or 20 years before that, so we 
call it a 100-year-old discipline. It really has evolved, but some of the core principles have not 
and have become timeless. 
If I have to distill the main principles for the discipline of value investing, I would say there are 
six in my mind. Three come directly from Ben Graham, the namesake of today’s lunch; one 
each from Warren and Charlie; and we add a small twist — you could call that the sixth. 
Here are the six basic principles in my mind that have guided our discipline, at least our 
practice, over the last 33 years. 
Ben Graham laid it out pretty quickly as he started this discipline with three basic ideas. A stock 
is a piece of ownership, not a piece of paper to trade around. Buying stock is really the same as 
buying a company. 
Secondly, the market is there to serve you, not to instruct you, which is a profound insight if you 
are in the midst of market activities. 
Thirdly, investing is about predicting the future, which is inherently unpredictable. Therefore, 
you always want to require a margin of safety that will help protect the downside as well as 
make a better upside. 
When Warren practiced, I think he added this further discipline, which I call a circle of 
competence. All of us are probably predisposed to have certain interests, and over time you 
develop particular expertise and try to study more and make it better. 
The most important concept of a circle of competence is knowing the edge of it, because most 
of us are wired to think we know a little more than we actually do. Understanding the edge is as 
important as understanding what is inside it. 
 
Page 4 
Charlie had this idea that you’ve got to fish where the fish are. He was a lifelong fisherman, and 
that is a wonderful analogy for the actual market. There are certain markets, industries, and 
businesses that draw a lot of attention. With that competition, your returns are averaged out. 
Then there are other industries, businesses, countries, or markets that don’t attract enough 
attention and have far fewer fishermen. You do way better to fish where the fish are. It’s a 
simple idea, but in practice it is amazingly effective. 
Lastly, over my own 33 years of practice as a global investor, applying the principles of value 
investing on a global basis at a time when global commerce is becoming one single market. 
One insight we have is that wealth, in the end, is really the percentage ownership of global 
purchasing power. 
It isn’t expressed, especially in the modern economy, in the amount of gold, diamonds, or 
currencies of any kind. With inflation, all of those will dissipate over time. What is important is 
what you can buy with it, what you can use it for. A better measurement of wealth is your 
percentage ownership of global purchasing power. 
The way we express that is by buying great businesses in the most dynamic economies at 
advantageous prices, waiting long enough for value to be created over time, and sharing 
proportionally in the upside. Here are the six basic ideas that I think can withstand the test of 
time and will serve everyone well. 
Tano: I like this last point very much. I’m already deviating from the script you and I agreed on, 
because I think going forward, keeping an eye on that purchasing power is going to be key if 
we’re not able to control inflation in the presence of these fiscal challenges. If we have time, 
we’ll come back to this. 
Li Lu: Sure. 
Tano: I want to get a question in before we run out of time, for the benefit of my students in the 
room. This is my prerogative as the person asking you the questions, so we’ll get this out of the 
way. 
Value investing as a practice has seen ups and downs. It’s been improving conceptually over 
time, with Bruce, your leadership, and many of the people in this room as well. What is the 
future of the equity analyst in the age of AI? Do you think we can still teach what we do at 
Columbia Business School going forward? 
Li Lu: Let me answer that in two parts. First, what investors do, and then let’s talk about AI 
separately. 
If you look at market participants, there are basically four different kinds of people. There are 
investors who stay with the company over time for value creation. 
 
Page 5 
There are also people who arbitrage the rights and wrongs of market pricing. In Ben Graham’s 
terms, as a realist, you buy from the pessimist and sell to the optimist. Those are the 
arbitrageurs. 
Then you have people who are in it mostly for speculation, mostly guessing what other people 
would buy or sell in a certain security. They don’t care about either the value pricing of the 
security or value creation. 
Then there are the brokers and market makers who facilitate all that. Most people are not 
necessarily purists. They encompass somewhat of all four. If you have indexing, it is exactly that 
average, in a sense. 
But value investors are into getting the right pricing discovery and waiting for value creation over 
a period of time. I would say Ben Graham was more of an arbitrageur, and Warren is using the 
arbitrage price, but mostly for value creation. 
The social benefit of all different ones is also quite interesting. Speculators, by definition, don’t 
stay there long enough for any of the value changes or creations, so they add up to roughly zero. 
Whatever is made and lost probably adds up exactly to that. Net to society, it is a cost to the 
functioning of the market. 
Brokerage and market making are also a cost to the functioning of the market. The market exists 
primarily for the goal of channeling excess savings into productive use, into deserving 
companies, and creating this modern economy that has compound economic growth. That is 
why the stock market exists in the first place. 
Why do you have this speculative side? It’s part of the human condition. Warren always 
describes the stock market as a church with a casino attached to it. The church is where the 
values are created, and the casino is almost part of the building permit, a necessary cost 
because of the human condition. Four hundred years ago, when it was created, this was how 
you inspired the animal spirit, and 400 years later it is still doing that. 
This is where you’re going to make a choice as students. Do you want to be in the zero-sum 
game, or the value creation game? That’s a personal choice. As a society, you also have a 
choice. You don’t want the casino side to be so out of proportion that it overwhelms the primary 
objective of why the market exists in the first place. 
Those are choices on the individual level as well as for society. Over 400 years, despite all this 
huge boom and bust, giant waste, somehow this mechanism has survived and continued to 
propel society as a core function. It is pretty miraculous, to say the least. 
For your students, it is important to make that distinction early on: What do you want to do 
personally? As a society, we should also calibrate the proportion of each. But they coexist as 
part of the human condition. 
 
Page 6 
Now, onto AI and the market. That’s a more complex question. First of all, what is AI, or this 
wave of generative AI? 
It is obviously a technology, a huge technological wave. As a technology, we’ve been dealing 
with that for the last few hundred years, ever since the Industrial Revolution. We have wave 
after wave of technological change, and the disruption and creation associated with it. Through 
that process of creative destruction, we understand some aspects of it. But somehow we feel 
this wave is different. Every wave is different, but this wave is unusually different from anything 
we’ve experienced so far. 
What makes it so different this time? On the surface, you can see the pace of change, the scale 
involved, and the concentrated financial impact at the top, the nature of that concentrated 
financial impact at the top. They’re all incredibly unprecedented. 
Then you ask why that is the case. The narrative is slightly different. Most of the time, until this 
moment, we’ve been dealing with technological changes as a fundamental tool for human 
productivity. 
With this technology, we introduce a different element. We now have a spectrum of tool versus 
creature, and we begin to change on that spectrum of tool versus creature. The moment it was 
first introduced, nearly four years ago, was the moment of the Turing test. At that point, we 
could no longer tell from language whether it was a machine or a human. 
From that point on, we were introduced to reasoning, and it began to gain more and more 
human features. From reasoning comes coding. With coding capability, it becomes an 
autonomously executing agent that functions much as a human does. Then comes the 
collaboration of all the agents in complex and long-lasting tasks—call that long reasoning. 
Much like human society, agents would organize, self-organize, prioritize, and execute tasks in 
an ever more sophisticated fashion, with their own language communication tools. That’s 
where we are. 
If you look at the Silicon Valley narrative, the generative AI will go to the stage of RSI, which 
we’re partially in – the idea that all the improvement would eventually be self-made, without a 
human in the loop. From RSI we will come to AGI, then ASI, the intelligence level exceeding all 
humans, individually as well as together. From there, you would say we’re creating somewhat of 
a semi-god or demigod, but a man-made creation. 
Because that is so powerful and all-encompassing, the economic impact, by definition, has to 
be huge and therefore justify all the different investment costs. When you have trillion-dollar 
IPOs, you’re all invited to participate in the IPO of a god or something. 
That is the narrative, and that is what makes it different. But if you step back and say – If this 
were indeed the case, what would become of humans? We would live in a society lorded over 
 
Page 7 
by a man-made god, accessed by very few and understood by none. Not even controlled – we 
can’t say that, because nobody understands it at that point. 
Is there anyone in humanity who would like to live in that society? My answer is probably a 
resounding no. I don’t think anyone would want to live in that society. 
There are only two outcomes, in a sense. A) This technology is not progressing in that direction, 
and we can discuss what it is and why it is not; or B) If it is indeed progressing in that direction, 
we will all, at some point, unite together to stop it from becoming that. In neither case are we 
going to have a man-made god living and lording over human society. 
That is what distinguishes this generation of technology, why it is different, and the different 
impacts, particularly the financial market impact. But leaving that aside, when you ask – Is this 
a useful technology? The answer is also a resounding yes. 
What is it, in essence? If I were to give it a provisional definition, from observing what it does 
and where it came from – Generative AI is a machine that by applying brute compute with clever 
algorithms, using all human-generated data and its first derivative, come up and establish  
systematic contextual correlations among near-infinite variables of human-generated data and 
its first derivative. In doing so, it establishes capabilities that include much of human reasoning 
and human intelligence. At present, we know how it works and how to make it better, but we 
don’t quite understand why it works, much as to the extent that we don’t quite understand how 
human machinery works.  
With that provisional definition, observing what is happening now, it equalizes a layer of the 
economy that is very helpful. If you look at the economy, at the bottom we have energy and 
transportation. On top of that sits manufacturing. On top of that, we have communication and 
digital media. Then we have an enormous amount of knowledge-based, technology-based 
services that synthesize all the knowledge we’ve accumulated and serve all the different layers 
of the economy. 
Generative AI today, at its current stage, is great at synthesizing and equalizing all the 
knowledge and expertise that has accrued to that layer, helping all the other ones. But it can’t 
change, for example, energy and transportation. It doesn’t change manufacturing, which is 
essentially the combination of different molecules and atoms and transforming them into 
different combinations. 
In communication and digitization, they’re already great synthesizers. That is the realm where it 
is going. It has not gone beyond humans. By this extension, it may not rise to whatever the 
narrative would dictate or lead you to believe. We’re still firmly within the human-generated 
data realm. 
To go to the biological sense requires a whole different level. For example, our—this may be 
going too far. 
 
Page 8 
Tano: Go for it. Knock yourself out. 
Li Lu: Each cell contains let’s say at least fifty petabytes of files, and you need to multiply that by 
trillions to get us on the biological level. We’re not anywhere close to getting to that level. 
But what has been established already begins to tip this balance between tool versus creature. 
One of the two arguments would persuade you to stop any further development without a 
human in the loop. 
RSI – recursive self-improvement – without a human in the loop would be very dangerous. They 
would develop goals and subgoals for their own purposes, and that would get them further from 
human control. [Who defines the “I” in RSI, humans or machines alone, that seems to me is a 
redline. Crossing it, we may not be able to get back.] 
In summary, this technology is enormously helpful, transformative, and extraordinarily 
dangerous. We have to, as a society and together as human beings, have a red line to firmly 
establish that whatever the self-learning or utilization of the tools, it cannot be without a human 
in the loop. In other words, firmly establish it on the tool side rather than the creature side. 
It’s also enormously disruptive, from employment to emotional dependency to risks from cyber 
to bio to nuclear. In the end, what you want society to develop is a balanced pace of 
development that balances benefit and risk. 
By the way, this technology will always have incremental costs. This is fundamentally different 
from the internet or a bunch of previous technologies, where you have a one-time investment 
and can amortize it for a long time. This is not the case. You always have an incremental cost 
associated with it. 
Cost, revenue, and profit are also very important. Capital needs and financial discipline will 
always be in operation. Also, the pace of development and the level of societal tolerance. You 
have four or five different layers of considerations for pacing and development into it. 
How does human society adapt to those kinds of changes? Not always by planning. We’re going 
to go through big boom and bust cycles, or even multiple ones. That is the nature of how it is 
going to develop. Those are the lines we have to think about as we approach this 
transformative, dangerous, disruptive, and costly technological wave. 
Tano: I think what you said, Li Lu, about this combination of being extraordinary, dangerous, 
and our not completely understanding why it is generating some of the answers it is generating, 
would require a human in the loop to check over it. 
Li Lu: Right. 
Tano: Once again, it’s going to be the scarce supply of this skill, of the person monitoring the 
artificial intelligence output, that will determine where rents are going to be located. 
 
Page 9 
Li Lu: That’s right. 
Tano: That effectively means if you’re smart and can communicate effectively with that AI 
inside any domain, you’re going to be the scarce resource, and probably the rents are going to 
accrue to you. Do I understand this correctly? 
Li Lu: I think that’s somewhere along those lines. It has different aspects and nuances, but I 
think that’s the case in the end. 
Tano: Let’s start projecting these ideas. One of the things that is most striking when we walk 
into the classroom—there are many of my colleagues here teaching capital markets, financial 
markets, value investing, investing in general—is that this is one peculiar market. 
I have a very vague question for you. The market seems to be driven by a very low number of 
companies that are pushing the technological frontier. The world seems dependent on these 
companies to push this frontier, and as a result, valuations are completely distorted by that. 
There’s a plot I show my students: the market capitalization of the company with the highest 
market capitalization, normalized by GDP. That number traditionally has been between 2 and 4 
percent. It is now about 15 percent with Nvidia. 
How do you think about this market, one that is becoming overly dependent on those few 
companies, with a very high beta to those companies? How do we design portfolios to protect 
ourselves against the shocks of this technology? 
Li Lu: The market always does peculiar things. 
Tano: Yes. 
Li Lu: From the very beginning, we go through this, and we’ll probably continue to do so. You 
don’t have to be dictated to by what the market decides to do at any given time. This is one of 
the most important insights and contributions from Ben Graham himself. 
At this point, if you look at the proposition of one recent prospectus that I read. Here’s a 
company that calls itself a research lab, yet it burns through tens of billions and promises to 
continue burning through hundreds of billions of dollars. It promises a transformative 
technology, but at the same time has a 10 percent chance of killing everyone. It wrote that in 
the prospectus and invited everybody to put in at least $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation. 
If there is there any inconsistency or irony?! Then this is. This is one extreme illustration of how 
irrational the market gets. It cannot both be true, but that’s where they are. It also tells you that 
things are not rational and not sustainable. Eventually, they won’t continue. Those are also the 
rules of the market, if you look throughout the centuries. 
 
Page 10 
They do strange things over a long period of time. Take the S&P since 2010, for example. In the 
last 16 years, it averaged 14 or 15 percent [of annualized return]. In the preceding 10 years, from 
2000 to 2010, it averaged exactly zero — in fact, slightly negative for 10 years. 
If you average the last 26 years, you get high single digits, and that is roughly right over the long 
term. If GDP grew in that period maybe 2 percent, and you have 2 to 3 percent inflation, you 
average about 4 to 5 percent nominal growth. 
Publicly listed companies do slightly better, especially those chosen by elimination to be the 
500 best companies. You come up with high single digits, and that is where the long-term 
average has been. 
That should serve as a basic grounding pillar of getting what you deserve and how the market 
rationalizes over a longer period. But it is punctuated by periods, sometimes long periods, when 
it goes to extremes. 
The example we just cited does strike people as, at a minimum, odd. That happens throughout 
history. If we ground society in the sense that a super-creature is simply not allowed or 
tolerated, it won’t go there. 
If it stays in the realm of tools, it will be like any other tool, with costs and benefits associated 
with it. Therefore, financial discipline and capital market discipline will eventually apply. The 
way you get there is through multiple ups and downs and boom and bust cycles, and that’s also 
fine. 
From that perspective, the bifurcation as a result of it — at any given time, you don’t create an 
enormous amount of new capital. If it is overwhelmingly driven to the top, that means you also 
have a whole bunch of otherwise wonderful businesses trading at very low prices. This is the 
same here, in China, or anywhere else. In China, it is probably more extreme, as some of the 
Chinese participants [in the room] would be well aware. 
Over time, the weight of the market will dictate the long-term returns of investors. You still get 
what you deserve in the end. There’s not much of a free lunch, even if it appears to be for a 
period of time, even a long period. Over the longer term, it will be weighed out by the natural 
weight of market rationalization itself. That’s why it has existed for a few hundred years already. 
I would say this bifurcation offers those with a rational mind a better opportunity set than at 
other times, if you stay rational, which is very difficult. It’s easy to get swept up, especially when 
you have a big technology wave. Your margin of imagination can expand dramatically. 
The speculative side of the market gets much more active, and the imagination becomes 
wilder, so the exaggerations tend to be more extreme. But for a rational mind, those create a 
better long-term opportunity set than otherwise. 
 
Page 11 
Tano: You mentioned China briefly there. Let’s talk a little bit about that. I just came back from 
China. I was teaching the participants in Hong Kong, and I took advantage of that occasion to 
do a couple of cases on Chinese companies and study the Chinese market a little. 
It’s been quite a ride over the last few years. How do you think about the Chinese market these 
days, with the problems in the Chinese economy associated with the real estate bust and the 
banking crisis? It looks reminiscent of some of the things we’ve seen in other places. How do 
you see investing in China these days? 
Li Lu: You mentioned the Chinese market. If you look at the last 10 years, it has basically been 
stagnant. What happened in those 10 years is fascinating. 
Ten years ago, the Chinese government had a decision to make. They had achieved somewhat 
of a middle-income level. The question was: How do we break away from it? So many countries 
have reached that level and stagnated there, so much so that there is a term to describe it – the 
middle-income trap. Dozens of countries achieved that and stayed there 40 or 50 years later. 
China is a large economy, so the question naturally is: What keeps a middle-income country 
stagnant and prevents it from breaking through the ceiling? You manufacture, you industrialize, 
you go with mid- to low-end manufacturing, but never break away from it. 
They had a decision to make. Do we want to break out, and can we do something to accelerate 
that process or make sure it happens? On its natural course, a lot of countries have failed to 
achieve that and stayed there for 40 or 50 years, some countries even longer. 
They embarked on this process of deliberately migrating the economy from low- to mid-end 
manufacturing into mid- to high-end manufacturing. Instead of a five-year plan, they had a 10-
year plan called Made in China 2025, in which they listed about 10 major objectives aimed at 
transforming Chinese basic manufacturing from low- to mid-end into mid- to high-end. 
A few years after that started, the first Trump administration came on board and started the 
trade war. This reinforced their idea that not only might they not break through that ceiling on 
their own natural course, but other countries might deliberately constrain them underneath it. 
The first Trump administration was followed by the Biden administration, which not only kept 
the trade tariffs but also added more technology restrictions. Five years into the 10-year plan, 
by 2021, the Chinese government doubled down on that direction. 
In addition to migrating manufacturing into the mid- to high-end, it added technological self-
sufficiency, particularly in areas where they had real bottlenecks: semiconductors, big aircraft 
engines, operating software code, and so on. There was a long list China was facing. That 
started another five years of doubling down and accelerating that process. 
When you try to achieve those impossible goals that so many countries have failed to achieve, 
it doesn’t come without deep and heavy costs. That has been the model by which China 
 
Page 12 
developed its economy. At different periods, they have big objectives and targets, with big costs 
associated with them. 
You mentioned real estate. In the last five years, one of the principal costs of achieving that goal 
has been the balance sheets and family wealth of middle-class Chinese families. By 2021, real 
estate prices reached their peak. A typical middle-class Chinese family had 70 percent of its 
net worth tied up in the home it owned. But that home carried roughly 50 percent leverage 
through a mortgage. 
In the next five years, until now, real estate prices nationwide lost about 40 percent of their 
value on average. They saw their entire family fortune go down 60 to 70 percent on average. 
When that happens, what do you do? You do three things: consume less, save more, and, to the 
extent possible, pay down debt. That is exactly what typical middle-class Chinese families have 
done over the last five years. 
Domestic demand has been growing slower and slower, to today roughly zero. Savings have 
gone up to about 120 percent of GDP, probably the largest savings deposits anywhere in the 
world, basically RMB 165 trillion. 
People have also been through two or three years of roughly zero price increases or slightly 
negative ones, more or less in that range. Therefore, they have a bit of a confidence issue when 
they look to the future. 
That is one tier of the economy. But if you look at the other tier, at the Chinese government’s 
objectives over the last 10 years and five years, you see a remarkably different picture. Chinese 
manufacturing has finally broken through from low- to mid-end, firmly into mid- to high-end. 
Every single objective of Made in China 2025 has been hit. In the last five years, solving the 
bottleneck issues has also made tremendous progress. Take the example of semiconductors. It 
turns out that the U.S.-led technology sanctions have been a godsend for the Chinese 
semiconductor industry because they have one of the most precious things in a market 
economy – DEMAND. 
Ask any entrepreneur what is most important, and they say the order book. If you have revenue, 
you get the whole ball rolling. With more revenue comes profit, comes R&D, comes better 
improvement, comes more revenue. That happened to the point that, on mature nodes, both 
the Chinese equipment side and fabrication side have achieved almost complete self-
sufficiency. On more cutting-edge, advanced nodes, they are getting close to self-sufficiency, 
with a few key missing ingredients. 
If you keep this way, on its natural course it will happen. That’s just one aspect. One of the key 
capabilities of generative AI is producing intelligence at scale on demand. One of the biggest 
applications is code generation, and that solves a big problem in some of those bottlenecks, 
primarily the missing layer of operating code systems. 
 
Page 13 
From PCs to servers to semiconductors to CUDA system of Nvidia, one by one, all of those are 
now being replaced with the help of AI. This becomes a great equalizer. 
Field after field, over the last 10 years, you’ve seen remarkable progress in migrating the basic 
contours of manufacturing from low- to mid-end to mid- to high-end. In some areas—new 
energy, EVs, storage, batteries, you name it, and it goes on and on, heavy machinery—they 
dominate. They have become global leaders. In areas where they have bottlenecks, they have 
also begun to migrate and close the gap. 
At the same time, it comes with very heavy costs to other industries. Real estate, for example, 
on an annual new sales basis, we’re now probably down about 70 percent. That RMB 10 trillion 
[in declining sales] is also exactly how much has been spent on manufacturing upgrading and 
technology efficiency, about RMB 10 trillion a year. If you look at the diversion, it is around 2021. 
That has been the development model if you look back over the last 50 years of China’s 
development. At any given time, roughly every 10 years or so in my mind, you get a new set of 
objectives and targets, and it comes with heavy costs. 
Sometimes in the next 10 years, the objective could become the cost. In the early days of 
industrial takeoff, the environment, air pollution, and rivers all became costs. In the proceeding 
next 10 years, they became the objectives, and new environmentally friendly technologies were 
developed. The polluters were the cost. 
In the course of urbanization, real estate developers were the objective, building China into 
what it is, with home ownership and firm middle-class wealth. In the last five or 10 years, they 
became the cost. 
You begin to suffer quite a bit, but overall you see the progress of the country through those 
periods. That is why you can compress development over a few hundred years into, say, 40 
years. But at any given time, as an investor or entrepreneur — and I’m sure all those people 
from China would strongly identify — you always want to know whether you are the objective or 
the cost. 
Being the cost of a state objective is no fun! I’m sure all of you intimately know that or have 
friends involved in the process. 
That’s how it has developed. Overall, if you give the score, you would say that, of all those 
changes, you now have a country of such size and population that has finally embarked on a 
complete course of modernization. But because of this two-tier economy and the general loss 
of confidence, you also have a financial market that has been stagnant for 10 years, going 
nowhere. 
Meanwhile, you have some of the greatest companies, globally competitive, trading at very low 
prices. Again, you have the bifurcation you see here. If you’re a rational investor and look at the 
whole picture, you might take a different perspective. 
 
Page 14 
I would say that in today’s market, you probably find a better opportunity set than you would at 
different times. That’s what you want. 
Tano: I’m going to take questions in a moment. While you get your questions ready, raise your 
hand. I want to ask you one last question, very quickly. 
You founded Himalaya Capital in 1997. I arrived at the University of Chicago about the same 
time as a young assistant professor. The world, at least to me — I don’t know how it looked to 
you then; we didn’t know each other — was very different, or looked very different from how it 
looks to me now. 
It was a world that was open, transnational, where with travel you could do so many things. It 
had, I don’t know how to say it, a generosity of spirit that seems to be a little lacking today. It 
looks very different to me now. 
How do you see it going forward, and do you incorporate any of those ideas into the way you 
think about investing? 
Li Lu: It’s a great question, Tano. The world has changed over the last 30 years. There’s no 
question about that. 
The world order, or the big questions of how the world governs and operates itself, changes on a 
slow scale. It takes decades, sometimes a hundred years, for an order to form and transform. 
The current world order was founded through two great world wars, which brought the whole 
world to the brink of collapse. Coming out of that, an American-led order emerged. Through the 
Cold War and the end of the Cold War, it became one order. Now it’s transforming once again 
into something yet to be seen, to emerge into what would emerge out of it. 
Underneath, there is another order that has been steadily forming for the last few hundred 
years: the economic order. It forms when more and more countries and populations join in 
common trade and transact business with each other. They form a common market. 
That common market was finally formed roughly 30 years ago, with the collapse of the Soviet 
Union and the end of the Cold War. Virtually all countries and populations began to join one 
market economy. 
What is interesting about this economic order is that, once a common market is formed, it is 
very difficult for any single country to withdraw voluntarily. Out of the market comes efficiency, 
comes the flywheel of continuous improvement along the lines of technology, efficiency, 
division of labor, trading of resources, and so on. Any country that withdraws for an extended 
period would face a great deal of cost. 
In the end, once it is formed, it is very difficult to disintegrate. It lasts much longer. Look at the 
trade wars and trade frictions over the preceding hundred years. No matter what frictions and 
 
Page 15 
barriers you erect, people find a way to trade through a third country, along the same principles 
of comparative advantage. 
Take U.S.–China trade. Of course, that has declined, but if you look at overall U.S. trade with 
Mexico plus ASEAN, they exactly offset it. Basically, U.S.–China trade remains the same, it just 
goes through a third-party country. That is roughly true in most other markets as well. 
In the political order, the U.S., having led the globe for 80 years and shouldered most of the 
costs of ensuring that the economic common market functions as it sees fit, began to realize 
that the costs and benefits derived from it were probably a bit out of proportion. It began to 
voluntarily withdraw some of those responsibilities, not very successfully so far, leaving a 
vacuum. 
The single biggest change in the political order is the rise of China over the last 30 or 40 years. It 
has become an enormous economic entity, with a complete set of manufacturing and 
technological self-sufficiency, and a single largest market that is also open, with unified 
regulation. 
That is a huge change to both the political and economic orders we are witnessing. At the same 
time, our mutual dependency, with one single market, has only increased, not decreased, over 
that period. 
I’ll give you one example. In generative AI, the one thing everybody needs is chips, 
semiconductor chips. Where are those chips being made? Think about all the countries that 
produce them. They have one thing in common. What do you think that might be? Sorry, I’m not 
putting you on the spot. 
Tano: I’m perfectly on the spot. Now I have to think about semiconductors when I was thinking 
that I need to open for questions. What do they all have in common? 
Li Lu: One thing in common among all the places that produce semiconductor chips essential 
for this technological wave, which the whole country seems to be betting on, is that every 
country and all the people who produce semiconductor chips use chopsticks. Think about that. 
Without exception. 
Tano: [laughter] 
Li Lu: Yes. Of course, all the people leading the semiconductor companies in this country also 
use chopsticks, from Jensen [Huang] to Lip-bu [Tan] to Lisa [Su], you name it, Hock [Tan], all of 
them. 
There is a great deal of mutual dependency, as you can see. If you’re betting to the extent we’re 
currently betting as a country and as companies on this new technology, whatever its promise 
and peril could be, then you have to be nice to people who use chopsticks. 
 
Page 16 
This is not changing. It didn’t happen by accident; we can go into why. There is a reason the 
president of the United States and the president of China find an urgency to meet four times in 
eight months. Two into it, the other two coming. The most important accomplishment of every 
meeting is that we schedule the next meeting. 
That comes the term strategic stability. In other words, stability is of strategic importance. I 
highlighted the sense of one global common market, the cost of withdrawing voluntarily from it, 
and mutual dependency deepening in a peaceful manner. 
Meanwhile, everybody is competing fiercely, all believing time is on their side. China to 
complete semiconductor self-sufficiency and all kinds of other things, the U.S. hoping for a 
breakthrough in AI and what it can promise. Other countries have different sets of calculations. 
It all highlights that peaceful stability is of paramount importance to everyone, of strategic 
importance. The largest countries have the responsibility and the desire to keep it that way. 
All countries would felt the weight of one single common market and the cost of withdrawing 
from it. The world, by and large, will continue to progress in that regard. The order we have been 
familiar with since the end of World War II is changing and transforming. What will emerge, and 
in what form, is yet to be seen. But the underlying formation of something with a more 
prominent impact, the forming of one single global common market, is here to stay. 
What is the implication for an investor? We come back to our basic tenets of value investing, 
the six principles. The last one we added is that, as a global investor, your wealth is expressed 
as your percentage ownership of global purchasing power. 
One way to accomplish that, certainly the way we’ve been practicing, is by buying great 
businesses in dynamic countries and markets at advantageous prices, and holding them for the 
long term to create value, preserve our percentage, and grow it over time. 
Back to Warren’s analogy describing the stock market as a church with a casino attached to it. 
What Berkshire has accomplished over the last 60 years is to build that church into a gigantic 
cathedral, which not only symbolizes and functions, but where people can find spiritual solace, 
because it provides the right function for which the market exists. 
What we’re trying to practice, back to your question, over the last 30 years, is that we want to 
prove that the gospel can be spread. We can build churches in other countries. We chose to 
build that church in Asia as well as other regions, as a global investor. Over time, some of those 
churches will appear in different countries, and some might grow into cathedrals as well. 
Let’s come back to your other question, to students and young professionals: What would you 
choose to do in this market? This is the basic setup, a church with a casino attached as part of 
the permitting process because of the human condition. 
 
Page 17 
They have different implications for the overall society. On one side, you have a win-win 
approach and a net benefit to society. On the other, you have zero-sum and a net cost, a net 
negative impact on society. 
The choices are yours. Technology, including AI, will remain a tool, not a replacement. If it has 
any tendency to replace humans, as I said, we will all unite to oppose such a creation of a man-
made god. 
Therefore, in my view, you don’t have to participate in a prospectus that calls it an IPO of a 
demigod. That is one way to express our collective duties to a good society. That’s why this 
program exists, and I think it ought to continue. Thank you very much. 
Tano: Thank you. 
 
Q&A 
Tano: We have 15 minutes for a couple of questions. All the way in the back—you were the first 
to raise your hand, so you get the right to do it. The only thing is that I’m going to ask you guys 
seriously to make it quick. 
Ed Lugo, EL2 Capital: Thank you again. I really appreciate it. I just want to get your sense of the 
difference between Chinese AI and American AI. Thank you. 
Li Lu: I’ll take two more questions at the same time. I will answer all three together. 
Tano: Who else were raising their hand. All the way in the back there. And someone here, too.  
Li Lu: We’ll do three questions at a time. 
Wenxuan Lu, Johns Hopkins: You mentioned the Chinese market. I want to hear your opinion 
about whether the Chinese stock market could be the objective or the cost. 
[Laughter] 
Tano: That’s a good question, actually. 
Li Lu: One more. 
Dan Bakalarz, Unison [Capital]: I’m curious how you underwrite political risk when the rules 
can change overnight, considering you’ve been so successful investing in Chinese businesses. 
Li Lu: The Chinese approach towards AI, whether the Chinese market is objective or cost, and 
how you underwrite political risk. They’re all connected, of course. 
If you describe the Silicon Valley approach to AI, the fundamental question is: What else can 
this technology do? That’s why they still call them research labs. I want to see what else it can 
do. How far can we push the edge of it? That’s why I also call it a frontier. 
 
Page 18 
The Chinese AI companies, I would say, are fundamentally curious about those questions as 
well. But in addition, and more importantly, they ask: What can this technology do for my 
customers, both my consumers and enterprise customers? 
There lies a very different approach. You can see from various metrics how the results will be 
different. 
The Chinese stock market — is that the objective or cost? At different times, the emphasis is 
different. But when you are the primary balance sheets of both individual families and the 
nation, when the real estate as a proportion begins to go down in one way, by the way, they 
don’t really go down forever because it has real value, then what in its place, would constitute 
the wealth of the nation, the people, and the families? 
When you answer that question, you would say that at some point, whether it’s today or 
another time, it [the market] has to be. That is the only asset that grows with the economy, in 
fact grows because of the economy, and is also the reason why the economy grows. They are all 
in a flywheel together. 
On political risk, that comes to do with understanding the objective at any given time, the 
history, and examining the record of all of it. That doesn’t just relate to China, it relates to the 
U.S. and a whole bunch of different questions. Our whole world is still somewhat organized 
around nation-states, and that’s the reality we live with. With all the considerations we talked 
about, we should apply that to all the countries in which we operate. 
Okay. Next set of questions. 
Daniel Qi, [Vita Specs]: Can you apply value investing principles and strategies to investments 
in growth companies or high-tech companies? Thank you. 
Moderator: The tech question. 
[Audience Questioner 5]: The second question I have is about the issue of energy convergence 
and intellectual capital, because energy markets are now very correlated with the consumption 
of knowledge-based businesses. I’m wondering whether this has implications for solving or 
creating problems involving climate issues, environmental issues, and others. I would also love 
to hear any thoughts you have on crypto markets in the context of global financial conditions. 
Tano: You got three questions in one, but we will forgive you. 
Hongming Li, Echt Capital: I’m a Columbia alumnus and already in the church of value 
investing and have been practicing for two years. The risk of underperformance in the 
investment business, where you try to preach value and see things slip away, holds real career 
risks. How do you think about it? 
Tano: That’s a wonderful question.  
 
Page 19 
Li Lu: There are five or six questions, somewhere there. Value investing principles and growth 
and technology companies; energy and all the associated implications for current AI, climate 
change, and somehow relating to crypto. 
Tano: You can do it, Li Lu. 
Li Lu: Sure. The third one is about underperformance and how you keep yourself in business, 
even though you’re two years into it. 
First of all, the value principle — I put it this way. I think all intelligent investment is value 
investment, because you always want to get a little more than what you pay for. What you pay is 
the price; what you get is value. 
Whatever value you can express yourself, whether it is in a business that is stagnant or even 
declining but pays you a whole bunch of money back, or a company that is rapidly growing, or a 
bet that has only a small percentage of winning and a large percentage of losing, therefore you 
spread [your bets] — all of that come down to your understanding of where value will be 
created. 
The basic principle is discounted future cash flow, to the extent that you can understand and 
estimate it accurately. They all come down to the same mathematics. That’s why I say almost 
all intelligent investing is value investing. The basic principle doesn’t change. You can apply it 
differently based on where your circle of competence is, going back to the concept Warren 
articulated so well. 
Energy is obviously essential, an essential layer of the economy. I see energy and 
transportation, manufacturing, communication, and then knowledge-based services. Those 
are essentially the entire economy. Of course, they have applications in every single layer. 
Of cause right now, the constraint on AI ranges from chips to electricity to labor. It applies 
differently, and it has an impact on climate. Any one of those subjects, we could go into almost 
endless aspects of it. 
But your third question, regarding your question about crypto, I have a very simple answer. I 
don’t think anything of it. I think eventually it will disappear on its own, and that’s okay, because 
it’s fundamentally bogus. 
If you think about what constitutes a currency that is redeemable, it is enforced because of the 
forces associated with it. Without that mechanism of enforcement, you cannot have any 
enforceable measure of settlement or store of wealth. Some guys creating it out of a garage 
doesn’t do the job. Yes, it helps criminals and facilitates all kinds of illicit transactions. 
I think we’re all better off banning it, but that’s okay. If somebody wants to collect it in the same 
way people think a certain artist is worth a certain price, that’s your personal preference. But as 
a society, I think nothing of it. It’s very simple. 
 
Page 20 
Now, your question [about the risk of underperformance] is very real. You’re buying into it, but 
then, of course, you also want to ask it to cooperate with you. 
As I said, that is where human psychology is. Everybody likes to have the best of both worlds. In 
fact, they want everything – I want to be doing win-win, but I also want to report good numbers 
every year at least, preferably every quarter, then every month, every day, every hour – Pretty 
soon, you will become a speculator. 
You cannot have both worlds. Either you think the market is there to instruct you, or you think 
the market is there to serve you. You can only take one of the two. Anyone who wants to 
mishmash all of it is better off indexing, because it is exactly the average of all the market 
participants. You average out those four kinds of market participants, that’s the index. You’re 
better off doing that. 
If you say – How do I make a business out of it? – In the end, you have to have people with a like-
minded approach who stick with you. 
The difficult thing about this line of work is that you have to be a bit contrarian in terms of 
human nature. You’ve got to have some element of a mutated genome to think you are right 
because logic and facts say so, not because anybody else agrees or disagrees with you. That 
requires a different kind of psychology. Some people fit it, if you decide you don’t, don’t even 
try. 
You also have to have people who believe in that to be along with you. Therefore, you cannot 
say – I want to have the biggest fund, have this AUM. – It doesn’t happen that way. You get what 
you deserve in the end. 
Tano: Let’s take a question from this side. 
Alex Capital, Cat Rock Capital: Hi, Li Lu. Thanks so much for doing this. You’ve been such a 
successful investor for such a long time. What have you learned in the last 10 years that you 
think are the most important lessons that make you a better investor today than you were 10 
years ago? 
If I can sneak in a second one: You keep your mind and body very sharp at 60 years old. You’re 
taking three questions at a time and remembering all the nuances. I’d love to hear about your 
daily or weekly routines to keep your mind and body [healthy] 
Li Lu: You got a few questions out there.  
Tano: This is like the Martha Stewart segment of the conversation, your diet and— 
Li Lu: Anybody else? 
[Audience Questioner 8]: My question is about structural changes in the U.S. and Chinese 
capital markets. 
 
Page 21 
Li Lu: Say that again? 
[Audience Questioner 8]: Looking ahead a decade or more, what are the most important 
structural changes in the U.S. and Chinese capital markets? Thank you. 
Tano: Say it in Chinese. I will translate.  
[Laughter] 
[Audience Questioner 8 translated from Chinese]: I’m asking about structural changes in the 
Chinese and U.S. capital markets. 
Tano: Now I got it. 
Li Lu: I’m still struggling. I’ll choose to understand whatever I can with my limited ability, now 
that I’m 60 years old. Thank you for reminding me. 
Li Lu: One more. Last one. 
Wyatt Neyman, First Manhattan: When you are underwriting an investment, how do you 
ensure you have an adequate margin of safety and downside protection? 
Li Lu: Where do you see the margin of safety, what have I learned in the last 10 years and how 
do I keep engaged this far, and structural changes between the U.S. and Chinese markets? I 
don’t know what that means, but I will say something along those lines. 
One of the distinguishing characteristics that separates a value investor from most other 
investors is the enormous attention paid to downside protection. 
Investing is predicting the future, which is inherently unpredictable. What you do is invest in the 
things you do know. What you know could be limited. Everybody starts with very limited known 
knowledge. That’s how I started when I was in my 20s. I didn’t know much. 
I go with the things I know are there. The balance sheet, obviously, as in Benjamin Graham’s 
work, because some things are easier to understand. 
Then I gradually progress from something simple to something less simple and more complex. 
It’s a natural progression in terms of the circle of competence. About circle of competence, one 
thing is to understand its edge. The other is consciously to expand it gradually over time. 
I always say, if you can compound your knowledge sustainably, eventually you can compound 
your capital as well. 
That goes back to your question about what I’ve learned over 10 years. Every 10 years, I find I’ve 
learned so much that you’re almost somewhat a different person. You want to have that 
renewed sense that, over a long period, if you do the right thing in the right way, it will be 
remarkable to find that you actually compound. 
 
Page 22 
This is another reason, I would say, if you want to choose to go to a win-win situation rather than 
zero-sum. You actually will compound your ability and knowledge, and perhaps your health, 
too. Maybe not quite, but you can at least prolong your productive span, your health span. 
Maybe not lifespan, but your health span. 
You keep engaged. It’s interesting. You know it’s helpful to society, and you’re not taking away 
from society. 
With the zero-sum game, the trouble is that a lot of human nature goes to zero-sum, to the 
short term. Whatever you learn today is useless tomorrow. You don’t accumulate. 
You rely more and more on the impersonal. You get a bigger computer, and now you use AI. 
You’ll be replaced at some point, so what is the value of that as a human? 
Of course, I like the human in the loop. I advocate learning, having an engaged and improved 
life over time, and compounding your knowledge as well as the capital of the people in the 
trusting way. 
What my mentor, partner, and teacher Charlie Munger always said and advocated is that the 
highest order of relationship he could discover is a seamless web of deserved trust. 
A seamless web of deserved trust! 
There lies a whole philosophy of approaching life in a productive way that is win-win for society 
as well. I recommend anyone starting your career to lean towards that way of life. 
It could take years. It could be slow, but slowly and surely you will get to where you deserve to 
go. That is a better way of living. 
Some people have a little more luck than others along the way. Our life, success, and failure are 
sometimes a combination of lucky or unlucky breaks in life. We’ve had a fair share of all of it. I, 
for one, never felt our record was completely our genius or anything. We’ve got so many lucky 
breaks along the way. 
But if you choose the right partners, the right approach, the right people to bet on, and the right 
things to do, over time it’s remarkable how compound returns work. 
The basic idea of compounding is that you don’t lose what you already have. That’s a profound 
idea. You don’t lose what you already have, including your knowledge, your trusting 
relationships, your wisdom, and even your health. Those are amazingly powerful things to have 
in life. 
In that regard, I think structurally the U.S. and China are the same. In fact, that’s the structure of 
humanity. That doesn’t necessarily answer your question, I’m sure. Maybe we’ll find another 
time to discuss exactly what you mean by structural changes. 
 
Page 23 
There are always changes in life. This is one constant we’re always going to have to deal with. 
You will always have your share of luck and unluck, and your share of great opportunities, no 
matter which way you naturally lean. 
Finding something you naturally lean towards and building on it over time in a compounded and 
cumulative fashion is just a better way of living a productive life. 
Tano: Thank you so much, Li Lu. This was wonderful! 
[Applause]

海尔布伦格雷厄姆与多德投资研究中心

第36届格雷厄姆与多德年度午餐会文字实录

日期：2026年10月5日

地点：纽约市大都会俱乐部

主持人：塔诺·桑托斯教授，哥伦比亚商学院罗伯特·海尔布伦资产管理与金融学讲席教授、海尔布伦格雷厄姆与多德投资研究中心学术主任

演讲嘉宾：李录，1996届校友（哥伦比亚学院1996届、法学院1996届），喜马拉雅资本创始人兼董事长

炉边对谈

塔诺：非常感谢。我知道大家来到这里都无比兴奋，而且我知道这不是因为我，而是因为我们今天的嘉宾，我马上就会介绍他。

在开始访谈之前，请让我花几分钟告诉大家，和每年这个时候一样，海尔布伦中心新学年的各项工作已经全面展开。在座的部分同学已经上过我的现代价值投资课。他们正在上应用价值投资课、信贷超级高速公路课，还有各种选修课。我们都非常享受其中。他们每一个人都特别出色。

此外，海尔布伦中心今年还有一项新举措。我们推出了首个全球价值投资者项目，这是与哥伦比亚商学院高管教育部门共同开展的项目，第一期学员今天就在这里。他们都是今年来访的中国朋友，非常优秀。非常感谢你们来到这里。

迈克尔［莫布森］和我——这个问题我被问得实在有点太频繁了——已经在筹备《与传奇人物共话价值投资》播客的新一季。新节目很快就会推出，大家可以期待一下。

We made our new stock selections for the student portfolio, the Tom Russo student portfolio. 
What did we buy this year? Equifax, Humana. What else? We bought the great Japanese bicycle 
company, Shimano, a classic value play if there was one; Copart, an online auction company; 
Perimeter Solutions, fire solutions [company]. A lot of fun things. As always, you can download 
all the reports the students have done over the years on the different companies. It’s a 
wonderful resource, and I very much encourage you to look at that. 
I want to single out a wonderful member of our community. I’m always amazed by Tom Russo’s 
generosity with the Heilbrunn Center, not only because of the student portfolio, but because of 
everything he does for the program, and in particular this year, making sure that our friend Li Lu 
could be here, for which we’re always thankful. 
We just had a wonderful week, as I told you a moment ago. With this new program, the Global 
Value Investor program, Andrew Gundlach and Kristin Gilbertson put on a show for them, which

and have become timeless. 
If I have to distill the main principles for the discipline of value investing, I would say there are 
six in my mind. Three come directly from Ben Graham, the namesake of today’s lunch; one 
each from Warren and Charlie; and we add a small twist — you could call that the sixth. 
Here are the six basic principles in my mind that have guided our discipline, at least our 
practice, over the last 33 years. 
Ben Graham laid it out pretty quickly as he started this discipline with three basic ideas. A stock 
is a piece of ownership, not a piece of paper to trade around. Buying stock is really the same as 
buying a company. 
Secondly, the market is there to serve you, not to instruct you, which is a profound insight if you 
are in the midst of market activities. 
Thirdly, investing is about predicting the future, which is inherently unpredictable. Therefore, 
you always want to require a margin of safety that will help protect the downside as well as 
make a better upside.

competence. All of us are probably predisposed to have certain interests, and over time you 
develop particular expertise and try to study more and make it better.

of us are wired to think we know a little more than we actually do. Understanding the edge is as 
important as understanding what is inside it.

李录：谢谢你，塔诺。首先，感谢大家来到这里。这真是一个非常美好的场合。当年我还是学生，以及刚步入职业生涯时，也参加过几次这样的午餐会。那是最令人期待的活动。30年后的今天，我希望自己的表现能不辜负这个场合。

价值投资这门学问起源于哥伦比亚大学。本·格雷厄姆最初开课，已经是将近90年前的事了。当然，在那之前他就已经实践了10年或20年，所以我们把它称为一门有着100年历史的学问。它确实一直在演变，但有些核心原则始终没有改变，并且已经变得历久弥新。

如果要我提炼价值投资这门学问的主要原则，我认为有六条。其中三条直接来自本·格雷厄姆，今天这场午餐会就是以他的名字命名的；沃伦和查理各贡献了一条；我们又加上了一点小小的延伸——你可以把它称为第六条。

在我看来，以下就是过去33年来指引我们这门学问，至少是指引我们实践的六个基本原则。

本·格雷厄姆在创立这门学问之初，很快就用三个基本理念把它阐述清楚了。股票是一份所有权，而不是一张供人买来卖去的纸。买股票实际上就等同于买一家公司。

第二，市场的存在是为了服务你，而不是指导你。如果你置身于市场活动之中，就会发现这是一条极其深刻的洞见。

第三，投资关乎预测未来，而未来本质上是不可预测的。因此，你始终都应该要求有一个安全边际，它既有助于防范下行风险，也能带来更好的上行收益。

我认为，沃伦在实践中又增加了这样一条纪律，我把它称为能力圈。我们每个人可能天生就对某些事物感兴趣，随着时间推移，你会培养出特定的专长，并努力进一步研究，让它变得更好。

能力圈这个概念最重要的一点，是知道它的边界在哪里，因为我们大多数人天生就会觉得自己懂得的比实际懂得的多一点。理解它的边界，和理解圈内的东西同样重要。

查理有一个观点，就是你得去有鱼的地方钓鱼。他一辈子都爱钓鱼，这是对现实市场的一个绝妙比喻。有些市场、行业和企业吸引了大量关注。在这样的竞争之下，你的回报会被拉平到平均水平。还有一些行业、企业、国家或市场没有吸引到足够的关注，钓鱼的人也少得多。到有鱼的地方钓鱼，你会做得好得多。这是一个简单的道理，但在实践中却有着惊人的效果。

最后，在我自己作为全球投资者的33年实践中，在全球商业正在成为一个统一市场的时代，我一直在全球范围内运用价值投资原则。我们得到的一个洞见是，财富归根结底实际上是你拥有的全球购买力份额。

尤其在现代经济中，财富并不体现为你拥有多少黄金、钻石或任何一种货币。随着通货膨胀，所有这些都会随着时间流逝而消减。重要的是，你能用它买到什么、能拿它做什么。衡量财富更好的方式，是你拥有的全球购买力份额。

我们将这个理念付诸实践的方式，是在最具活力的经济体中，以有利的价格买入优秀企业，等待足够长的时间，让价值随着时间推移而创造出来，并按所持份额分享上行收益。这就是我认为能够经受时间考验、让每个人都从中受益的六个基本理念。

塔诺：我非常喜欢最后这一点。我已经开始偏离我们事先商定的提纲了，因为我认为，展望未来，如果我们在面对这些财政挑战时无法控制通货膨胀，那么密切关注购买力就会成为关键。如果有时间，我们会再回到这个话题。

There are also people who arbitrage the rights and wrongs of market pricing. In Ben Graham’s 
terms, as a realist, you buy from the pessimist and sell to the optimist. Those are the 
arbitrageurs. 
Then you have people who are in it mostly for speculation, mostly guessing what other people 
would buy or sell in a certain security. They don’t care about either the value pricing of the 
security or value creation. 
Then there are the brokers and market makers who facilitate all that. Most people are not 
necessarily purists. They encompass somewhat of all four. If you have indexing, it is exactly that 
average, in a sense. 
But value investors are into getting the right pricing discovery and waiting for value creation over 
a period of time. I would say Ben Graham was more of an arbitrageur, and Warren is using the 
arbitrage price, but mostly for value creation. 
The social benefit of all different ones is also quite interesting. Speculators, by definition, don’t 
stay there long enough for any of the value changes or creations, so they add up to roughly zero. 
Whatever is made and lost probably adds up exactly to that. Net to society, it is a cost to the 
functioning of the market. 
Brokerage and market making are also a cost to the functioning of the market. The market exists 
primarily for the goal of channeling excess savings into productive use, into deserving 
companies, and creating this modern economy that has compound economic growth. That is 
why the stock market exists in the first place. 
Why do you have this speculative side? It’s part of the human condition. Warren always 
describes the stock market as a church with a casino attached to it. The church is where the 
values are created, and the casino is almost part of the building permit, a necessary cost 
because of the human condition. Four hundred years ago, when it was created, this was how 
you inspired the animal spirit, and 400 years later it is still doing that. 
This is where you’re going to make a choice as students. Do you want to be in the zero-sum 
game, or the value creation game? That’s a personal choice. As a society, you also have a 
choice. You don’t want the casino side to be so out of proportion that it overwhelms the primary 
objective of why the market exists in the first place. 
Those are choices on the individual level as well as for society. Over 400 years, despite all this 
huge boom and bust, giant waste, somehow this mechanism has survived and continued to 
propel society as a core function. It is pretty miraculous, to say the least. 
For your students, it is important to make that distinction early on: What do you want to do 
personally? As a society, we should also calibrate the proportion of each. But they coexist as 
part of the human condition.

a period of time. I would say Ben Graham was more of an arbitrageur, and Warren is using the 
arbitrage price, but mostly for value creation. 
The social benefit of all different ones is also quite interesting. Speculators, by definition, don’t 
stay there long enough for any of the value changes or creations, so they add up to roughly zero. 
Whatever is made and lost probably adds up exactly to that. Net to society, it is a cost to the 
functioning of the market. 
Brokerage and market making are also a cost to the functioning of the market. The market exists 
primarily for the goal of channeling excess savings into productive use, into deserving 
companies, and creating this modern economy that has compound economic growth. That is 
why the stock market exists in the first place. 
Why do you have this speculative side? It’s part of the human condition. Warren always 
describes the stock market as a church with a casino attached to it. The church is where the 
values are created, and the casino is almost part of the building permit, a necessary cost 
because of the human condition. Four hundred years ago, when it was created, this was how 
you inspired the animal spirit, and 400 years later it is still doing that. 
This is where you’re going to make a choice as students. Do you want to be in the zero-sum 
game, or the value creation game? That’s a personal choice. As a society, you also have a 
choice. You don’t want the casino side to be so out of proportion that it overwhelms the primary 
objective of why the market exists in the first place. 
Those are choices on the individual level as well as for society. Over 400 years, despite all this 
huge boom and bust, giant waste, somehow this mechanism has survived and continued to 
propel society as a core function. It is pretty miraculous, to say the least. 
For your students, it is important to make that distinction early on: What do you want to do 
personally? As a society, we should also calibrate the proportion of each. But they coexist as 
part of the human condition.

但价值投资者致力于发现正确的价格，并在一段时间内等待价值创造。我会说，本·格雷厄姆更多是一位套利者，而沃伦也利用套利价格，但主要是为了价值创造。

不同类型参与者带来的社会效益，也很有意思。按照定义，投机者不会停留足够长的时间，去经历任何价值的变化或创造，所以他们合计的结果大致为零。所有赚到和亏掉的钱，加在一起很可能恰好就是零。对社会而言，其净效应是市场运行的一项成本。

经纪和做市同样也是市场运行的一项成本。市场存在的主要目的，是把多余的储蓄引导至生产性用途，引导到值得投资的企业，并创造出这种能够实现复利式经济增长的现代经济。这就是股市最初存在的原因。

为什么又会有投机这一面呢？这是人性的一部分。沃伦总是把股市形容成一座附带赌场的教堂。教堂是创造价值的地方，而赌场几乎可以说是建筑许可的一部分，是由于人性而不得不付出的必要成本。400年前，当它被创立时，人们就是这样激发动物精神的，而400年后，它仍然在发挥这样的作用。

作为学生，你们要在这里作出选择。你想参与的是零和游戏，还是价值创造的游戏？这是个人的选择。作为一个社会，你同样也有选择。你不会希望赌场这一面的比例失衡到如此地步，以至于压过了市场最初存在的主要目的。

这些既是个人层面的选择，也是社会层面的选择。400年来，尽管经历了所有这些巨大的繁荣与萧条、惊人的浪费，这套机制还是以某种方式存活了下来，并且继续发挥核心作用，推动社会前进。至少可以说，这相当神奇。

对于你的学生来说，尽早分清这两者非常重要：你个人到底想做什么？作为一个社会，我们也应当调节各自所占的比例。但它们作为人性的一部分，是共存的。

现在来谈人工智能与市场。这是一个更复杂的问题。首先，什么是人工智能，或者说，这一波生成式人工智能是什么？

它显然是一项技术，是一场巨大的技术浪潮。作为技术，自工业革命以来，过去几百年我们一直都在应对这类事情。我们经历了一波又一波的技术变革，以及随之而来的颠覆与创造。在这个创造性破坏的过程中，我们理解了其中的某些方面。但不知为什么，我们觉得这一次浪潮不一样。每一波浪潮都有所不同，但这一波与我们迄今经历过的任何事情相比，都显得格外不同。

这一次究竟有什么如此不同？从表面上看，你能看到变化的速度、涉及的规模，以及集中在头部的财务影响，还有这种集中在头部的财务影响的性质。这些都空前得令人难以置信。

接着你会问，为什么会这样？这次的叙事略有不同。在此之前的大多数时候，我们所应对的技术变革，都是提升人类生产力的一种基本工具。

而这项技术引入了一个不同的因素。现在，我们面前出现了一条从工具到生物的连续谱，而且我们开始在这条工具与生物的连续谱上发生移动。将近四年前，它首次出现的那一刻，就是图灵测试的时刻。在那个时点，我们已经无法仅凭语言判断对方是机器还是人。

从那以后，推理能力被带到了我们面前，它开始获得越来越多的人类特征。从推理又发展出编程。有了编程能力，它就成为能够自主执行任务的智能体，运作方式与人类十分相似。接着，就是所有智能体协作执行复杂而持久的任务——可以把这称为长时推理。与人类社会非常相似，智能体会进行组织、自我组织、确定优先级，并以越来越复杂精细的方式执行任务，而且有它们自己的语言交流工具。这就是我们目前所处的位置。

如果看看硅谷的叙事，生成式人工智能将发展到RSI阶段，我们已经部分进入了这个阶段——其理念是，最终所有改进都会由它自己完成，不再需要人类参与其中。从RSI，我们将走向AGI，然后是ASI，其智能水平将超越所有人类，无论是单个人，还是全体人类加在一起。从那一步开始，可以说，我们在创造某种半神，或者说次神，但这是一个人造的存在。

因为它如此强大、无所不包，按定义来说，其经济影响必然极其巨大，因此也就足以证明各种投资成本的合理性。当出现万亿美元级别的首次公开募股时，大家都被邀请去参与一位神，或者类似什么存在的首次公开募股。

这就是那套叙事，也正是它使这一次与众不同。但如果你退后一步问：如果事情果真如此，人类会变成什么样？我们将生活在一个被

Is there anyone in humanity who would like to live in that society? My answer is probably a

What is it, in essence? If I were to give it a provisional definition, from observing what it does 
and where it came from – Generative AI is a machine that by applying brute compute with clever 
algorithms, using all human-generated data and its first derivative, come up and establish  
systematic contextual correlations among near-infinite variables of human-generated data and 
its first derivative. In doing so, it establishes capabilities that include much of human reasoning 
and human intelligence. At present, we know how it works and how to make it better, but we 
don’t quite understand why it works, much as to the extent that we don’t quite understand how 
human machinery works.  
With that provisional definition, observing what is happening now, it equalizes a layer of the 
economy that is very helpful. If you look at the economy, at the bottom we have energy and 
transportation. On top of that sits manufacturing. On top of that, we have communication and 
digital media. Then we have an enormous amount of knowledge-based, technology-based 
services that synthesize all the knowledge we’ve accumulated and serve all the different layers 
of the economy. 
Generative AI today, at its current stage, is great at synthesizing and equalizing all the 
knowledge and expertise that has accrued to that layer, helping all the other ones. But it can’t 
change, for example, energy and transportation. It doesn’t change manufacturing, which is 
essentially the combination of different molecules and atoms and transforming them into 
different combinations. 
In communication and digitization, they’re already great synthesizers. That is the realm where it 
is going. It has not gone beyond humans. By this extension, it may not rise to whatever the 
narrative would dictate or lead you to believe. We’re still firmly within the human-generated 
data realm. 
To go to the biological sense requires a whole different level. For example, our—this may be 
going too far.

人造的神统治的社会里，只有极少数人能够接触它，却没有任何人能够理解它。甚至谈不上控制——我们不能这么说，因为到了那一步，没有人理解它。

人类当中，有谁愿意生活在这样的社会里吗？我的回答大概会是一个响亮的“不”。我不认为有任何人愿意生活在这样的社会里。

从某种意义上说，只有两种结果。A）这项技术并没有沿那个方向发展，我们可以讨论它究竟是什么，以及为什么它不会如此发展；或者B）如果它确实正沿那个方向发展，我们所有人都会在某个时刻团结起来，阻止它变成那样。无论哪种情况，都不会有一位人造的神存在于人类社会之中并统治人类社会。

这就是这一代技术的独特之处，是它与众不同的原因，也是它产生不同影响，尤其是金融市场影响的原因。但先把这些放在一边，如果你问：这是一项有用的技术吗？答案同样是一个响亮的“是”。

它本质上是什么？如果根据我对它所做的事情及其来源的观察，给出一个暂定定义——生成式人工智能是一种机器，它将大规模蛮力计算与巧妙的算法相结合，利用人类生成的全部数据及其一阶衍生数据，在这些人类生成的数据及其一阶衍生数据中近乎无穷的变量之间，找出并建立系统性的上下文相关关系。在这个过程中，它建立起了包含人类推理和人类智能诸多方面的能力。目前，我们知道它是如何运作的，也知道如何让它变得更好，但我们并不十分理解它为什么有效，就像我们在很大程度上也并不十分理解人类这套机制是如何运作的一样。

基于这个暂定定义，再来观察当下正在发生的事情，它正在拉平经济中某一层的差异，这非常有帮助。如果看看整个经济体系，最底层是能源和交通运输。其上是制造业。再往上，是通信和数字媒体。然后，我们有大量基于知识、基于技术的服务，它们整合我们积累的所有知识，为经济中的各个不同层面提供服务。

今天的生成式人工智能，在其目前这个阶段，非常擅长整合这一层积累的全部知识和专业技能，并将其普及，从而帮助其他所有层面。但它无法改变比如能源和交通运输。它也不改变制造业，制造业本质上是把不同分子和原子加以组合，再把它们转化为不同的组合。

在通信与数字化方面，它们已经是很出色的整合者。那就是它正在进入的领域。它还没有超越人类。沿着这种延伸方向，它未必会达到那套叙事所宣称、或者所引导你相信的高度。我们仍然牢牢处在人类生成数据的范围之内。

要进入生物学意义上的那个层面，需要达到一个完全不同的水平。比如，我们的——这可能说得有点远了。

But what has been established already begins to tip this balance between tool versus creature. 
One of the two arguments would persuade you to stop any further development without a 
human in the loop. 
RSI – recursive self-improvement – without a human in the loop would be very dangerous. They 
would develop goals and subgoals for their own purposes, and that would get them further from 
human control. [Who defines the “I” in RSI, humans or machines alone, that seems to me is a 
redline. Crossing it, we may not be able to get back.] 
In summary, this technology is enormously helpful, transformative, and extraordinarily 
dangerous. We have to, as a society and together as human beings, have a red line to firmly 
establish that whatever the self-learning or utilization of the tools, it cannot be without a human 
in the loop. In other words, firmly establish it on the tool side rather than the creature side. 
It’s also enormously disruptive, from employment to emotional dependency to risks from cyber 
to bio to nuclear. In the end, what you want society to develop is a balanced pace of 
development that balances benefit and risk. 
By the way, this technology will always have incremental costs. This is fundamentally different 
from the internet or a bunch of previous technologies, where you have a one-time investment 
and can amortize it for a long time. This is not the case. You always have an incremental cost 
associated with it. 
Cost, revenue, and profit are also very important. Capital needs and financial discipline will 
always be in operation. Also, the pace of development and the level of societal tolerance. You 
have four or five different layers of considerations for pacing and development into it. 
How does human society adapt to those kinds of changes? Not always by planning. We’re going 
to go through big boom and bust cycles, or even multiple ones. That is the nature of how it is 
going to develop. Those are the lines we have to think about as we approach this 
transformative, dangerous, disruptive, and costly technological wave.

李录：假设每个细胞都包含至少50拍字节的文件，而要达到我们在生物层面的水平，你还需要把它乘以数万亿。我们离那个层面还差得非常远。

但已经建立起来的能力，开始让工具与生物之间的这架天平发生倾斜。那两个论点中的一个，会说服你停止任何没有人类参与其中的进一步发展。

RSI，也就是递归自我改进，如果没有人类参与其中，将会非常危险。它们会为自己的目的制定目标和子目标，这将使它们进一步脱离人类控制。［RSI中的“I”（改进）究竟由谁来定义，是人类，还是机器独自定义？在我看来，这似乎是一条红线。一旦越过，我们可能就再也回不来了。］

总而言之，这项技术有着极大的帮助，具有变革性，同时也极其危险。作为一个社会，作为共同生活的人类，我们必须划定一条红线，明确确立这样一个原则：无论是自我学习还是工具的使用，都不能没有人类参与其中。换句话说，必须把它牢牢定位在工具这一端，而不是生物那一端。

它也有着巨大的颠覆性，从就业到情感依赖，再到网络、生物乃至核方面的风险。最终，你希望社会形成一种均衡的发展速度，在收益与风险之间取得平衡。

顺便说一句，这项技术永远都会有增量成本。这与互联网或此前许多技术有着根本不同，后者只需一次性投入，就可以在很长时间内摊销。而这项技术并非如此。你始终都会有与之相关的增量成本。

成本、收入和利润也非常重要。资本需求和财务纪律将始终发挥作用。此外，还有发展的速度，以及社会的容忍程度。对于它的发展速度与发展进程，你需要考虑四五个不同层面的因素。

人类社会如何适应这些变化呢？并不总是通过规划。我们将经历巨大的繁荣与萧条周期，甚至可能不止一次。这就是它发展过程的本质。在面对这一波具有变革性、危险性、颠覆性，而且成本高昂的技术浪潮时，这些就是我们必须思考的方向。

塔诺：李录，我认为，你刚才所说的这几种特征结合在一起——它非同寻常，又很危险，而且我们还不能完全理解它为什么会生成它所生成的某些答案——就意味着必须有人类参与其中，对它进行检查。

李录：没错。

塔诺：再一次，将决定经济租金落在哪里的，是这种技能的稀缺供给，是那些监督人工智能输出的人的稀缺供给。

Tano: Let’s start projecting these ideas. One of the things that is most striking when we walk 
into the classroom—there are many of my colleagues here teaching capital markets, financial 
markets, value investing, investing in general—is that this is one peculiar market. 
I have a very vague question for you. The market seems to be driven by a very low number of 
companies that are pushing the technological frontier. The world seems dependent on these 
companies to push this frontier, and as a result, valuations are completely distorted by that. 
There’s a plot I show my students: the market capitalization of the company with the highest 
market capitalization, normalized by GDP. That number traditionally has been between 2 and 4 
percent. It is now about 15 percent with Nvidia. 
How do you think about this market, one that is becoming overly dependent on those few 
companies, with a very high beta to those companies? How do we design portfolios to protect 
ourselves against the shocks of this technology? 
Li Lu: The market always does peculiar things. 
Tano: Yes. 
Li Lu: From the very beginning, we go through this, and we’ll probably continue to do so. You 
don’t have to be dictated to by what the market decides to do at any given time. This is one of 
the most important insights and contributions from Ben Graham himself. 
At this point, if you look at the proposition of one recent prospectus that I read. Here’s a 
company that calls itself a research lab, yet it burns through tens of billions and promises to 
continue burning through hundreds of billions of dollars. It promises a transformative 
technology, but at the same time has a 10 percent chance of killing everyone. It wrote that in 
the prospectus and invited everybody to put in at least $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation. 
If there is there any inconsistency or irony?! Then this is. This is one extreme illustration of how 
irrational the market gets. It cannot both be true, but that’s where they are. It also tells you that 
things are not rational and not sustainable. Eventually, they won’t continue. Those are also the 
rules of the market, if you look throughout the centuries.

李录：没错。

塔诺：这实际上意味着，如果你足够聪明，并且能够在任何一个领域内有效地与那个人工智能沟通，你就会成为稀缺资源，经济租金大概也会归你所有。我理解得对吗？

李录：我想，大致就是这个意思。其中有不同的方面和细微差别，但我认为最终是这样的。

塔诺：我们来进一步推演这些想法。我们走进课堂时，最令人吃惊的事情之一——在座有很多我的同事，教授资本市场、金融市场、价值投资以及一般意义上的投资——就是，这是一个非常奇特的市场。

我有一个很笼统的问题想问你。市场似乎是由极少数正在推动技术前沿的公司所驱动的。世界似乎依赖这些公司来推动这个前沿，因此，估值也被完全扭曲了。

我会给学生看一张图：市值最高的那家公司的市值，除以国内生产总值（GDP）。这个数字历来介于2%到4%之间。现在，以英伟达而言，这个数字大约是15%。

你如何看待这样一个市场：它正在变得过度依赖那几家公司，对这些公司的贝塔系数非常高？我们应该如何设计投资组合，来保护自己免受这项技术所带来的冲击？

李录：市场总是会做出奇怪的事情。

塔诺：是的。

李录：从一开始，我们就在经历这些事情，而且很可能还会继续经历下去。在任何一个特定时刻，市场决定做什么，你都不必任其摆布。这是本·格雷厄姆本人最重要的洞见和贡献之一。

就眼下而言，看看我最近读到的一份招股说明书所提出的主张。这是一家自称研究实验室的公司，却烧掉了数百亿美元，还承诺要继续烧掉数千亿美元。它承诺带来一项具有变革性的技术，但与此同时，这项技术有10%的可能性会杀死所有人。它把这一点写进了招股说明书，然后邀请大家按2万亿美元的估值，投入至少1000亿美元。

如果说有什么前后不一致或讽刺之处？！那就是这个。这是市场会变得多么不理性的一个极端例子。这两件事不可能同时成立，但这就是他们所处的状态。这也告诉你，这些事情既不理性，也不可持续。最终，它们不会继续下去。如果你纵观几百年的历史，就会发现，这同样是市场的规律。
